name: Pramlintide

lead: Pramlintide is an injectable copy of amylin, approved by the US FDA in 2005 as an add-on to mealtime insulin in type 1 and type 2 diabetes. In fat-loss circles it is noted because insulin-treated patients lost weight rather than gaining it.

It slows stomach emptying, reduces glucagon after meals and increases satiety, so you feel full sooner and eat less. Trials showed modest improvements in HbA1c along with weight loss, and obesity research has looked at it in combinations such as with metreleptin.

paras: It is prescribed as a mealtime injection alongside insulin. Use for leanness is off-label, and it is not approved for obesity.
The US label carries a boxed warning for severe hypoglycemia when used with insulin. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Pramlintide is an approved amylin analogue that slows stomach emptying and raises fullness, so you eat less and lose weight. Insulin-treated patients in diabetes trials lost weight rather than gaining it. Use for leanness is off-label.

lead: Pramlintide (brand name Symlin) is a synthetic analogue of amylin, a hormone released by pancreatic beta cells with insulin. The US FDA approved it in March 2005 as an add-on to mealtime insulin in people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes who have not reached glucose targets.[1][2] It is injected subcutaneously.

Amylin slows gastric emptying, promotes satiety and reduces glucagon secretion.[1][3] In trials of insulin-treated patients, pramlintide lowered HbA1c modestly and was associated with weight loss rather than the weight gain typical of insulin.[4][5] Its weight effect has been studied in obesity research, including in combination with metreleptin, but it is not approved for obesity.[6][7] Its US label carries a boxed warning for severe hypoglycemia when used with insulin.[2]

paras: The labelled indication is adjunctive treatment in type 1 or type 2 diabetes in people who use mealtime insulin and have not achieved desired glucose control.[2] Weight loss is an observed effect in trials but not a labelled use.

Pramlintide is an analogue of human amylin. Per the label, amylin is co-secreted with insulin after meals; the analogue slows gastric emptying, suppresses postprandial glucagon and increases satiety.[2][3] Amylin acts at receptors formed from the calcitonin receptor and receptor activity-modifying proteins.[3][8] Rat-amylin residues were substituted to make the analogue less prone to forming amyloid.[1]

The label boxed warning states that use with insulin raises the risk of severe hypoglycemia, particularly in type 1 diabetes, usually within three hours of injection, and advises insulin dose reduction and careful patient selection.[2]

One-year randomized trials of pramlintide added to insulin in type 1 and type 2 diabetes reported improvements in glycemic control with reduced or stable body weight.[4][5][4] An earlier randomized study with open-label extension in type 1 diabetes examined long-term efficacy.[9] A phase 2 exploratory study registered pharmacodynamic effects in obese subjects.[10] Preclinical work found synergistic fat-specific weight loss from amylin plus leptin in rats, and a clinical study of pramlintide with metreleptin reported enhanced weight loss compared with either alone.[6][7] A systematic review lists insulin-associated weight gain as the problem such adjuncts address.[11]
Pramlintide is prescription-only in the US.[2] No notable looksmaxxing-community discussion was found; its interest for fat loss stems from amylin-class research.[3]

timeline.event: Randomized study and extension in type 1 diabetes published.[9]
Preclinical and clinical amylin-leptin synergy reported.[6]
